cards.explanation: The answer is Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Ahaziah, king of Samaria, tells his messengers, “Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury.” He fell through a lattice, and he sends messengers to ask a god of Ekron. I've been in a drawer, and even I know you ask the right One. (2 Kings 1:2)

The question is, “Is there no God in Israel?” The angel of the LORD tells Elijah the Tishbite to ask, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?” Elijah doesn't ask where they're headed or who sent them. He asks the one question that points straight at the problem, friends. And that question is going to come back around again. (2 Kings 1:3)

The answer is that he will surely die. The LORD says it plainly: “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” Ahaziah sent messengers to ask a god of Ekron whether he would recover. The word that came back was from the LORD, through Elijah, whom the angel of the LORD sent to meet the messengers. That's the kind of answer you can't get anywhere else. (2 Kings 1:3-4)

The answer is False. The messengers hold nothing back, friends. They tell the king that a man came up to meet them and said, “Go back to the king who sent you and tell him that this is what the LORD says…” Then they pass along every word, down to “You will surely die.” Whatever the king is about to feel, they delivered the message in full. (2 Kings 1:6)
The answer is True. The messengers say, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist.” And the king answers, “It was Elijah the Tishbite…” Two details, and he's got a name. (2 Kings 1:8)

The answer is that the king says come down. The captain goes up to Elijah, who is sitting on top of a hill, and says, “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down!’…” He calls Elijah a man of God, then hands him an order from the king. Remember that, friends, because those two things don't sit together well. (2 Kings 1:9)

The answer is True. The second captain says, “Come down at once!” and Elijah answers, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” That's exactly what he said to the first captain. The only change is on the king's side, where the order becomes “Come down at once!” (2 Kings 1:11-12)

The answer is that the fire of God consumes them. After Elijah speaks, “…the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” It's a heavy moment, friends, and I'll say that once and plainly. The text calls it the fire of God. (2 Kings 1:12)

The answer is that he falls on his knees and begs. The third captain goes up, “…fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him…” No orders this time, no “Come down!” at all. He comes asking instead of telling. (2 Kings 1:13)

The answer is that his life and his men's would be spared. He says, “Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” Then he adds, “But now may my life be precious in your sight.” He points to what happened to the first two captains, and he asks for his life and his men's lives. (2 Kings 1:13-14)

The answer is afraid. The angel of the LORD says to Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” That's a lot of men and a lot of fire behind this moment, and the angel tells Elijah to go down anyway. I think that's a comfort, friends, because the angel of the LORD is the one who says to go. (2 Kings 1:15)

The answer is False. Elijah tells the king, “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” And the king doesn't get up. The text says, “So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken.” When the LORD says it, it happens. (2 Kings 1:16-17)

The answer is Jehoram. Ahaziah had no son, so Jehoram takes the throne of Israel after him. Now here's the part that tangles people up, friends. There's another Jehoram too, the son of Jehoshaphat, who reigns over Judah, and the text uses his reign to mark the year. Same name, two kings, and I still can't keep two cookie cutters straight on a busy day. (2 Kings 1:17)
